title: What anti-corruption training do the DOJ and SEC expect under the FCPA?
description: What the DOJ and SEC FCPA Resource Guide expects of anti-bribery training, and how the 2025 enforcement pause and guidelines affect it, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) does not itself mandate training, but the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Resource Guide to the FCPA names "training and continuing advice" as a hallmark of an effective compliance program. They look for periodic training and certification for directors, officers, relevant employees and, where appropriate, agents and business partners, tailored to the audience and in the local language, plus a way to get urgent compliance advice.
keyTakeaways: The Resource Guide (Second Edition, July 2020) is joint DOJ Criminal Division and SEC Enforcement Division guidance; it is non-binding and does not create rules, but it describes how both agencies assess compliance programs.

Training expectations: periodic training and certification for all directors, officers and relevant employees, and agents and business partners where appropriate; content on policies, applicable law, real-life scenarios and case studies; audience-specific delivery in the local language.

Training also appears in the third-party hallmark (periodic training and annual certifications for third parties), in remediation (focus future training on lessons learned), and in acquisitions (train new employees promptly).

Executive Order 14209 (February 10, 2025) paused new FCPA investigations for review, and the Deputy Attorney General's June 9, 2025 guidelines now govern which cases DOJ pursues; the statute itself is unchanged.
For financial institutions, FCPA training usually sits beside AML and sanctions training, and the DOJ evaluates all of them under its Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs.
regulator: US Department of Justice (DOJ), Criminal Division, Fraud Section FCPA Unit; US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Division of Enforcement, for issuers
appliesTo: Issuers with securities registered or reporting obligations in the United States (15 U.S.C. 78dd-1), including listed banks, insurers and asset managers
Domestic concerns: US companies and US citizens, nationals and residents (15 U.S.C. 78dd-2)
Foreign persons acting while in the territory of the United States
Issuers' books and records and internal accounting controls obligations under 15 U.S.C. 78m(b)(2)

sections.heading: Where do the FCPA training expectations come from?

blocks.text: They come from [A Resource Guide to the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/criminal-fraud/file/1292051/dl?inline), prepared by the DOJ Criminal Division and the SEC Enforcement Division. The first edition appeared in November 2012 and the Second Edition in July 2020. The FCPA's anti-bribery provisions and its accounting provisions say nothing about training, so the expectation is a matter of enforcement policy rather than statutory duty.

The Guide is explicit about its status: it is "non-binding, informal, and summary in nature" and does "not constitute rules or regulations." Its weight comes from the fact that both agencies consider the adequacy of a company's compliance program when deciding whether to bring a case, what to charge and how to resolve it. For issuers, the internal accounting controls provision in 15 U.S.C. 78m(b)(2)(B) gives compliance controls, including training, a direct statutory anchor.

The DOJ's more detailed questions about training, such as how training is tailored, tested and updated after incidents, are in its Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs, covered separately in [DOJ compliance program training expectations](/regulations/doj-compliance-program-training-expectations). This page focuses on what is specific to the FCPA.

sections.heading: What does the Resource Guide say about training?

blocks.text: The Guide says policies only work if they are communicated, and that the agencies will check whether that has happened through periodic training and certification across the organization, including outside parties where appropriate.

blocks.title: FCPA Resource Guide, Training and Continuing Advice
blocks.text: "DOJ and SEC will evaluate whether a company has taken steps to ensure that relevant policies and procedures have been communicated throughout the organization, including through periodic training and certification for all directors, officers, relevant employees, and, where appropriate, agents and business partners."

items: **Content:** training "typically covers company policies and procedures, instruction on applicable laws, practical advice to address real-life scenarios, and case studies."
**Delivery:** many larger companies mix web-based and in-person training "at varying intervals"; the Guide sets no fixed frequency.

**Audience:** information should be presented in a manner appropriate for the targeted audience, including training materials in the local language. The Guide's example is different training for sales personnel and accounting personnel, with hypotheticals close to what they face.
**Continuing advice:** beyond training, a company should provide guidance on its ethics and compliance program, "including when such advice is needed urgently."

blocks.text: The absence of a fixed frequency matters for design. Annual training is common practice, but the Guide's test is whether the program is understood and followed at all levels, which pushes toward more frequent or deeper training for roles with government touchpoints, third-party approvals or payment authority.

sections.heading: Where else does training appear in the Resource Guide's hallmarks?

blocks.text: Training recurs in three other hallmarks: third-party management, remediation after misconduct, and integration of acquisitions. The Guide's hallmarks of effective compliance programs also cover senior management commitment, codes and policies, oversight and resources, risk assessment, incentives and discipline, confidential reporting and investigation, and periodic testing.

blocks.caption: Training expectations across the FCPA Resource Guide hallmarks (Second Edition, July 2020)
head: Hallmark
Training expectation in the Guide
rows: Periodic training and certification for directors, officers, relevant employees, and agents and business partners where appropriate
Ongoing monitoring of third parties may include "providing periodic training, and requesting annual compliance certifications by the third party"
Investigation, Analysis, and Remediation of Misconduct
Integrate lessons learned into policies, training and controls, which requires analysis of root causes
After an acquisition, companies "should consider training new employees", reevaluating third parties and auditing new business units
Effort should follow risk: the Guide contrasts a $50 million government contract in a high-risk country with modest routine gifts

blocks.text: The Guide's compliance program case study involves a US-based financial institution whose real estate transactions with a Chinese state-owned entity were corrupted by its own executive. The institution had "frequently trained its employees" and had "provided extensive FCPA training to the senior executive responsible for the transactions." DOJ and SEC declined to take enforcement action against the institution, while the executive pleaded guilty. Targeted training of the person in the high-risk role was part of the record that earned the declination.

sections.heading: How did the 2025 executive order and DOJ guidelines change FCPA enforcement?

blocks.text: They narrowed which cases DOJ pursues, but left the statute and the Resource Guide in place. [Executive Order 14209](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/02/14/2025-02736/pausing-foreign-corrupt-practices-act-enforcement-to-further-american-economic-and-national-security), signed February 10, 2025, directed the Attorney General to review FCPA enforcement for 180 days, to cease initiating new FCPA investigations during that period unless an individual exception was made, and to issue updated guidelines.

On June 9, 2025 the Deputy Attorney General issued [Guidelines for Investigations and Enforcement of the FCPA](https://www.justice.gov/dag/media/1403031/dl?inline). New FCPA investigations must now be authorized by the Assistant Attorney General for the Criminal Division or a more senior official. Prosecutors are told to prioritize misconduct linked to cartels and transnational criminal organizations, conduct that deprived identifiable US companies of fair competition, and threats to national security, and not to focus on "de minimis or low-dollar, generally accepted business courtesies." The guidelines direct focus on "substantial bribe payments", sophisticated concealment, fraud and obstruction tied to particular individuals.

blocks.title: What this means for training
blocks.text: The guidelines change enforcement priorities, not the law, and enforcement policy can change again while past conduct remains chargeable. The guidelines also point prosecutors to the Foreign Extortion Prevention Act (18 U.S.C. 1352), which criminalizes foreign officials' demands for bribes. Training that teaches staff to recognize and escalate high-value, concealed or intermediary payments matches the current priorities; reducing anti-corruption training on the strength of the 2025 changes would be a risk decision, not a legal conclusion.

sections.heading: How can a financial institution map FCPA expectations to training evidence?

blocks.text: The practical question is what a firm could hand the DOJ or SEC to show the training hallmark was met for the people and third parties involved in a transaction. The mapping below is illustrative.

blocks.text: Evidence of understanding is stronger than evidence of attendance; see [how to evidence training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator). For linking each row to the obligation it serves, see [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

sections.heading: How does FCPA training fit with other financial crime training at a bank or asset manager?

blocks.text: Bribery, money laundering and sanctions risks often arise in the same relationships, so many institutions combine the governance while keeping distinct learning outcomes. Corrupt proceeds are a money laundering risk under the Bank Secrecy Act program, and sanctions screening sits under the [OFAC sanctions compliance training](/regulations/ofac-sanctions-compliance-training) expectations.

Global firms also face foreign regimes with their own adequate procedures tests, such as Australia's offense of [failure to prevent foreign bribery](/regulations/failure-to-prevent-foreign-bribery-training). A single anti-corruption framework with jurisdiction-specific modules usually serves better than separate programs. More on the sector's obligations is on the [financial services industry page](/industries/financial-services).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps the Resource Guide hallmarks and the institution's corruption risk assessment to roles, third parties and transactions before any course is written, so training for a relationship manager differs from training for an accounts payable clerk. Each certification and scenario assessment stays linked to the hallmark it evidences, which is the record DOJ and SEC ask to see.

faqs.q: Does the FCPA legally require anti-corruption training?
faqs.a: No. Neither the anti-bribery provisions nor the accounting provisions require training. The DOJ and SEC Resource Guide treats training and continuing advice as a hallmark of an effective compliance program, and the agencies weigh program effectiveness when deciding whether and how to resolve a case.

faqs.q: How often should FCPA training happen?
faqs.a: The Resource Guide asks for "periodic" training and notes that larger companies train "at varying intervals"; it sets no fixed frequency. Annual training is common, with more frequent or targeted training for people in high-risk roles or transactions, as in the Guide's financial institution case study.

faqs.q: Was the FCPA repealed or suspended in 2025?
faqs.a: No. Executive Order 14209 of February 10, 2025 paused the initiation of new DOJ FCPA investigations for a review period, and DOJ's June 9, 2025 guidelines now govern which cases it pursues. The statute remains in force, and the guidelines require Criminal Division leadership to authorize new investigations.

faqs.q: Should third parties receive FCPA training?
faqs.a: Where appropriate, yes. The Resource Guide includes agents and business partners in its training hallmark and suggests that ongoing monitoring of third parties may include periodic training and annual compliance certifications by the third party.

factCheck.claim: Resource Guide Second Edition prepared by DOJ Criminal Division and SEC Enforcement Division, dated July 2020, first edition November 2012; 'non-binding, informal, and summary in nature' and does not constitute rules or regulations.

Training and Continuing Advice hallmark: verbatim sentence on periodic training and certification for directors, officers, relevant employees, agents and business partners; mix of web-based and in-person at varying intervals; content list; local language; sales vs accounting example; advice when needed urgently.

Third-party hallmark: ongoing monitoring may include periodic training and annual compliance certifications; remediation: integrate lessons learned into policies, training and controls; M&A: consider training new employees; risk assessment $50 million contract example.

Compliance Program Case Study: US-based financial institution frequently trained employees, provided extensive FCPA training to the responsible senior executive; DOJ and SEC declined enforcement against the institution; executive pleaded guilty.
Executive Order 14209 signed February 10, 2025 (90 FR 9587): 180 day review, cease initiation of new FCPA investigations absent individual exception, issue updated guidelines; extendable by 180 days.

DAG memo June 9, 2025: new FCPA investigations must be authorized by the AAG Criminal Division or more senior official; factors include cartels/TCOs, harm to identifiable US companies, national security, serious misconduct; not focus on de minimis or low-dollar generally accepted business courtesies; references Foreign Extortion Prevention Act 18 U.S.C. 1352.
